newsitem.title: USA: Chicago firm trades OTC stocks like listed ones.
newsitem.headline: Chicago firm trades OTC stocks like listed ones.

text.p: A small specialist firm in Chicago is hoping to make a big splash in the U.S. securities market by trading over-the-counter stocks on the floor of the Chicago Stock Exchange (CHX).
Stock market analysts and traders said the firm could find cracking a market that has been characterized by long-standing relationships and set ways of doing business very difficult.
"God bless 'em if they make a profit," the head of one equities desk in New York said.
He added that the "if" was a big one.

Melvin Specialists, the only minority-owned specialist firm on a listed stock exchange in the U.S., began trading shares of such Nasdaq names as Coventry Corp, Fiserv Inc and Liposome Co at the beginning of May.
"It's an interesting experiment," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp.

"What they're trying to do is to put a little twist in these things and show that putting a listed stock, auction market flavor to those (OTC) stocks will attract order flow and therefore they'll make money," Johnson said.
"They're going to have to show markets that are competitive with OTC," he added.
William Lilliwitz, a managing director at Melvin, said the firm has a higher risk profile than regular OTC market makers by being on a regulated exchange floor.

Exchange market makers facilitate trades and provide liquidity by either buying or selling, taking the other side of a trade when it comes in. OTC dealers have somewhat more leeway than market makers in buying or selling.

Typically, OTC stocks are traded on the Nasdaq stock market, which is a computer-based trading system devoid of the open outcry, auction system on which stocks listed on exchanges such as the CHX and New York Stock Exchange trade.

"Our main focus in getting involved in this business was the fact that we saw the marketplace changing in the last four, five months to reflect the need for Nasdaq stocks to be traded more like listed stocks," Lilliwitz said.
Earlier this year, Nasdaq began offering tighter bid/ask spreads on its stocks amid a drive by regulators to make the market more accessible to retail investors.
Melvin is not the first CHX-based firm to trade OTC stocks on the floor of the exchange, but the other four firms doing so have done it mainly on a proprietary basis.
Robert Forney, president and chief executive officer of the CHX, said two of the four firms trading OTC stocks have been doing so for more than eight years.
"We've had some success with certain issues and amazing success" with others, he said.
First Albany's Johnson said one key for Melvin to succeed will be to build relationships with investment firms in order to get order flow going their way.
Lilliwitz said the firm has commitments from some of the larger brokerage houses in New York.
"The stocks that we're busy in have been reasonably small at this point in terms of business, but we're starting to make some headway" from some regional firms as well, he added.
Forney said the OTC program started on a pilot basis but was expanded after consultations with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission.
"Now there are five firms and a total of around 300 issues that they'll be trading shortly," he said, adding that the exchange has SEC approval to trade up to 500 OTC stocks.
"We've got good firms that are doing it and we'll just see how it works out," he said.
